🐛 Describe the bug
The following program proves an illegal memory access whereas the version without torch.compile works.
import torch

@torch.compile
def indexit(A, b):
    return A[b - 1]

A = torch.rand(20)
b = torch.zeros(4)

print(indexit(A, b))

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/scratch/zdevito/pytorch/hi.py", line 11, in <module>
    print(indexit(A, b))
  File "/scratch/zdevito/pytorch/torch/_tensor.py", line 426, in __repr__

    return _str_intern(self, tensor_contents=tensor_contents)
  File "/scratch/zdevito/pytorch/torch/_tensor_str.py", line 567, in _str_intern

  File "/scratch/zdevito/pytorch/torch/_tensor_str.py", line 327, in _tensor_str

  File "/scratch/zdevito/pytorch/torch/_tensor_str.py", line 115, in __init__
    nonzero_finite_vals = torch.masked_select(
RuntimeError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
CUDA kernel errors might be asynchronously reported at some other API call, so the stacktrace below might be incorrect.
For debugging consider passing CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1.
Compile with `TORCH_USE_CUDA_DSA` to enable device-side assertions.

Inductor kernel:
@triton.jit
def triton_(in_ptr0, in_ptr1, out_ptr0, xnumel, XBLOCK : tl.constexpr):
    xnumel = 4
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    x0 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x0), xmask)
    tmp1 = 1
    tmp2 = tmp0 - tmp1
    tmp3 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (tmp2), xmask)
    tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x0 + tl.zeros([XBLOCK], tl.int32)), tmp3, xmask)

Note that indexing by -1 is valid and means to read the last element similar to python, but the code being generated here does not appear to have any handling for this case.
This bug has been running in the GPT2ForSequenceClassification benchmark for some time but is covered up by the fact that slight reads off the end of tensors do not always generate illegal memory faults.

🐛 Describe the bug
When one torch.compile()'s the optimizer.step() for the following models and optimizers on CPU, inductor generates a C++ kernel that takes in too many arguments for ctypes to handle and hits a "ctypes: too many arguments" error (microsoft/nnfusion#399). The compiled optimizer step kernel unrolls the for loop of updates so that there are num params copies of the same code. The more parameters there are, the more likely it is to hit the error. Since it is just unrolling for-loops and the param updates do not interfere, the fix here would be to break up the kernels so that each take fewer arguments to avoid the error.

🐛 Describe the bug
To track following:

           // See https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/50937#issuecomment-779272492 
        

        
          
           #if AT_MKL_ENABLED() && (!defined(_WIN32))

           #endif 
        
    
  


Copy-n-paste from 2y.o comment:
What's wrong there
The following error message is generated in the Windows build jobs for this PR (e.g. this one)
error LNK2038: mismatch detected for 'RuntimeLibrary': value 'MT_StaticRelease' doesn't match value 'MD_DynamicRelease' ...

Root cause
The implementation of mkl_sparse_d_create_csr and mkl_sparse_destroy uses malloc/new and free/delete possibly, which requires UCRT. Currently, we link against the static variant of MKL with our code with /MD. With MSVC, you cannot have two copies of UCRT for a shared library / executable with different runtime library options (/MD and /MT).
Possible solutions
Solution 1
Remove the usages of mkl_sparse_d_create_csr and mkl_sparse_destroy
I don't know whether this is possible. But if possible, this is the easiest solution.
Solution 2
Link against the dynamic variant of MKL instead.
In this solution, we have two choices.
Choice A
We depend on package managers completely.
But the difficulty is that MKL doesn't provide every release of MKL in PyPI and Anaconda Cloud. e.g.  on PyPI, they have 2021.01 and 2019.0. However, on Anaconda Cloud, they have 2020.02 (defaults channel), 2020.04 (conda-forge channel) and 2021.01 (intel channel). So it is quite difficult for us to select the version of MKL to build PyTorch.
Another difficulty is that Anaconda Cloud doesn't provide the full set of development package for Windows. But we can install them through other package managers, e.g. nuget and choco.
Choice B
We copy the DLLs into the PyTorch package.
But the MKL DLLs are quite large. Uncompressed: 650M, Compressed: 128M
Choice C
A tradeoff between Choice A and B. But this still doesn't seem perfect.

import torch
import torch._dynamo

class Repro(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, batch_size,):
        super(Repro, self).__init__()
        self.hidden_size = int(hidden_size)
        self.input_size = int(input_size)
        self.batch_size = batch_size

        self.foo = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros((1,)))

        self.register_buffer("h_init", torch.zeros(1, self.hidden_size))

    def next_ht(self, ht):
        return ht * self.foo

    def forward(self, x):
        ht = self.h_init.broadcast_to((self.batch_size, self.hidden_size))
        for _ in range(x.shape[1]):
            ht = self.next_ht(ht)
            # ht = ht * self.foo
            torch._dynamo.graph_break()

        return ht

🐛 Describe the bug
The following program produces inconsistent results under eager mode and compile mode. Details for debugging are explained in the code. Note that we need a specific input tensor to trigger this issue (it may be not the only input that leads to inconsistency).
import torch

def fn(x):
    return torch.fmod(x, 2.3)
    # "✔️" means that the program works fine with the substitution.

🐛 Describe the bug
At the moment, the custom autograd function I defined (that performs in-place operation) fails gradcheck. You can reproduce the behaviour by running the below code.
import torch


class CustomMulBeta(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x, beta):
        ctx.beta = beta
        x.mul_(beta)
        ctx.mark_dirty(x)
        return x

    @staticmethod
    def jvp(ctx, x_eps, beta):
        x_eps.mul_(ctx.beta)
        return x_eps


inputs = torch.rand(
    (10, 10), dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True
)
beta = 3
torch.autograd.gradcheck(
    CustomMulBeta.apply,
    (inputs.clone(), beta),
    check_forward_ad=True,
    check_backward_ad=False,
    check_undefined_grad=False,
    check_batched_grad=False,
)

🐛 Describe the bug
There appears to be a severe performance issue with unique and unique_consecutive when return_counts=True and the device is mps. I performed the following test:
import timeit

import torch

t = torch.randint(10, size=(100000,), device='mps')
t = t[t.argsort()]
t_cpu = t.cpu()

number = 10

print(timeit.timeit('t.unique()', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t.unique(return_inverse=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t.unique(return_counts=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t_cpu.unique()', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t_cpu.unique(return_inverse=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t_cpu.unique(return_counts=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))
print()
print(timeit.timeit('t.unique_consecutive()', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t.unique_consecutive(return_inverse=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t.unique_consecutive(return_counts=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t_cpu.unique_consecutive()', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t_cpu.unique_consecutive(return_inverse=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))
print(timeit.timeit('t_cpu.unique_consecutive(return_counts=True)', globals=globals(), number=number))

nodes.bodyText:
repro:
@torch.compile
def f():
    a = torch.ones(2, device='cuda')
    torch.cuda.set_device(1)
    return a

print(f())

In eager that returns a tensor on the cuda:0 device, while the above repro returns a tensor on cuda:1.
@ngimel pointed out that inductor uses the device stored on the node metadata to figure out how to set device guards in the codegen (`node.meta['val'].device)
What's probably happening is set_device() is not part of ATen. So when AOTAutograd traces the dynamo graph into an ATen graph, it directly calls set_device(1) instead of putting it into the graph. Ideally, we'd want some way of plumbing the info about the set_device() call into inductor
cc @ezyang @soumith @msaroufim @wconstab @ngimel

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
torch.nn.Linear/torch.nn.functional.linear returns incorrect results for some shapes when using the MPS backend. It seems that the number of errors increases with the input size. Here is a reproducer:
import torch.nn as nn

def print_stats(y, y_p):
    abs_diff = (y - y_p).abs()
    items_different = (abs_diff > 1e-3).int().sum()

    print(
        f"linear diff sum: {abs_diff.sum()}"
    )
    print(
        f"items different (> 1e-3): {items_different} ({100*(int(items_different) / y.numel())}%)"
        )


x_cpu = torch.rand((253, 144, 768), dtype=torch.float32)

# This works, it seems like if you go higher than 129 in
# the second dimension, the errors start piling up.
# x_cpu = torch.rand((253, 129, 768), dtype=torch.float32)

linear_cpu = nn.Linear(in_features=x_cpu.shape[-1], out_features=3 * x_cpu.shape[-1])
linear_cpu.eval()
y_cpu = linear_cpu(x_cpu)

x_mps = x_cpu.to("mps")
linear_mps = linear_cpu.to("mps")

print("=== MPS Linear ===")
y_mps = linear_mps(x_mps)
print_stats(y_mps.to("cpu"), y_cpu)

print("=== MPS matmul ===")
y_mps_matmul = x_mps @ linear_mps.weight.t() + linear_mps.bias
print_stats(y_mps_matmul.to("cpu"), y_cpu)

Output:
=== MPS Linear ===
linear diff sum: 2246469.5
items different (> 1e-3): 8421751 (10.033140841918582%)
=== MPS matmul ===
linear diff sum: 5.270101547241211
items different (> 1e-3): 0 (0.0%)

As stated in the comments, everything works fine with an input of shape (253, 129, 768), however, once the second dimension is increased to 130 part of the output is erroneous.
When manually inspecting the output, it seems that the trailing rows are incorrect (they just have repeating float patterns).

🐛 Describe the bug
I've found some issues in the torch.norm MPS implementation:

(A) When executing with dim=[] and then executing with dim=1, the result is different from the CPU implementation.
(B) Conversely, when executing with dim=1 and then executing with dim=[], it causes a crash.

Code to reproduce issue (A):
import torch

v_cpu = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]])

norm_cpu = v_cpu.norm(2, dim=[])
norm_mps = v_mps.norm(2, dim=[])
print(f"v_mps.norm(2, dim=[]) = {norm_mps} should be {norm_cpu}")

v_cpu = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]])
v_mps = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]], device="mps")
norm_cpu = v_cpu.norm(2, dim=0)
norm_mps = v_mps.norm(2, dim=0)
print(f"v_mps.norm(2, dim=0) = {norm_mps} should be {norm_cpu}")

🐛 Describe the bug
ProcessGroupNCCL's watchdog is observed failing to crash a program when a collective times out.
This leads to the job being stuck without being noticed and hence wastes machine capacity.
Example program: hang.py
(expected to hang since rank 0 has more elements to all-reduce)
# Copyright (c) Meta Platforms, Inc. and affiliates
import argparse
import os
import time
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import datetime


def run_worker(rank, world_size):
    ndev = torch.cuda.device_count()
    device = torch.device(f'cuda:{rank % ndev}')
    torch.cuda.set_device(device)
    dist.init_process_group('nccl', rank=rank, world_size=world_size,
                            timeout=datetime.timedelta(seconds=10)
                           )

    numel = 100 * 1024 * 1024
    if rank == 0:
        numel *= 2
        print(f'Rank {rank} is the problematic rank')

    tensor = torch.ones(numel, device=device)
    dist.all_reduce(tensor)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(f"Rank {rank} completed\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    world_size = int(os.getenv("WORLD_SIZE", 8))
    rank = int(os.getenv("RANK", -1))
    run_worker(rank, world_size)
Launch command:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=8  --nnodes=1 hang.py

Output:
Rank 0 is the problematic rank
Rank 4 completed
Rank 5 completed
Rank 3 completed
Rank 6 completed
Rank 2 completed
Rank 7 completed
Rank 1 completed
[E ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:464] [Rank 0] Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: WorkNCCL(SeqNum=1, OpType=ALLREDUCE, Timeout(ms)=10000) ran for 10917 milliseconds before timing out.
Rank 0 completed
[E ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:478] Some NCCL operations have failed or timed out. Due to the asynchronous nature of CUDA kernels, subsequent GPU operations might run on corrupted/incomplete data.
[E ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:483] To avoid data inconsistency, we are taking the entire process down.

Although the log reports the timeout and claims to take down the process, it seems that TorchX is not being notified, as no RuntimeError is caught by TorchX.
Versions
master as of today

🐛 Describe the bug
currently torch in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blame/a37b4fa03a68115c25cf37bf2d5fac8f4f252e04/torch/_inductor/utils.py#L566
checks if torch.cuda.get_device_properties(index).multi_processor_count < 80
with the intention to check if there are sufficient cuda cores.
but the issue is that multi_processor_count has nothing to do with cuda cores at all, its the number of streaming multiprocessors on gpu.
and of course, it fails on quite a few gpus thus making torch.compile() unavailable to majority of users.
for example, rtx3060 has 28 streaming multiprocessors while it has 3584 actual cuda cores.

nodes.bodyText:
The json files produced when using torch.profiler.tensorboard_trace_handler with AMD GPUs have some problems.  The software setup has : torch==2.1.0.dev20230303+rocm5.4.2, and torch-tb-profiler==0.4.2, and the test system has AMD MI-250 GPUs.  The json files contain a number of records with category = kernel, name = Marker, but there are no GPU kernels named "Marker".   The json files also include a large number of records with category = kernel, but the events are not GPU kernels.  In addition, for compatibility with analysis with tensorboard, the category for "kernel" should be "Kernel", with an upper case K.
PyTorch profiles are produced using :
    with torch.profiler.profile(
             activities=[ torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CPU, torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CUDA ],
             schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=waitvalue, warmup=2, active=10, repeat=1),
             on_trace_ready=torch.profiler.tensorboard_trace_handler('/path/to/profiles'),
             record_shapes=True
    ) as torch_profiler:

Here is an example of a "kernel" record where the category should be something else, not a GPU kernel :
{
"ph": "X", "cat": "kernel", "name": "CopyHostToDevice", "pid": 2, "tid": 0,
"ts": 1679332639271782, "dur": 11,
"args": {
"External id": 8938
}
},
Here is an example of a "kernel" record with name = "Marker" :
{
"ph": "X", "cat": "kernel", "name": "Marker", "pid": 2, "tid": 1,
"ts": 1679332639305911, "dur": 363875,
"args": {
"External id": 10302,"Kernel": "void at::native::modern::elementwise_kernel<at::native::AUnaryFunctor<float, float, float, at::native::binary_internal::MulFunctor >, at::detail::Array<char*, 2> >(int, at::native::AUnaryFunctor<float, float, float, at::native::binary_internal::MulFunctor >, at::detail::Array<char*, 2>)", "grid dim": [1024, 1, 1], "block dim": [256, 1, 1], "shared size": 0, "stream": "0x0"
}
},
The json files also contain records for the "kernel" category where the kernel name and parameters are listed :
{
"ph": "X", "cat": "kernel", "name": "ncclKernel_SendRecv_RING_SIMPLE_Sum_int8_t(ncclDevComm*, unsigned long, ncclWork*)", "pid": 2, "tid": 1,
"ts": 1679332639718731, "dur": 30559,
"args": {
"External id": 10570,"Kernel": "ncclKernel_SendRecv_RING_SIMPLE_Sum_int8_t(ncclDevComm*, unsigned long, ncclWork*)", "grid dim": [4, 1, 1], "block dim": [256, 1, 1], "shared size": 0, "stream": "0x9928530"
}
},
but even in these cases the kernel name re-appears in the "args" list.
The json files produced when running the same PyTorch code with NVIDIA GPUs don't have these issues, but those files should specify category "Kernel" instead of "kernel" for the records corresponding to actual GPU kernels, so that tensorboard can properly identify the events.
Please update PyTorch profiler support for AMD GPUs with torch.profiler.tensorboard_trace_handler .

Currently updating triton pin is more involved than it should be, due to frequent errors in triton wheel build scripts that have some hardcoded versions. A lot of hardcoding has been fixed by @malfet (thanks!), with hopefully last bit being fixed in #96730.
We need relatively frequent triton updates, as a lot of bug fixes and perf improvements are happening there. Ideally, devinfra should handle infra parts of the update (making sure that wheels are building) with inductor team fixing test errors that appear due to moving pin.
I anticipate moving pin approx every 2 weeks, but can be more or less frequent depending on whether critical bugs are discovered. Some fixes critical bugs can be cherry-picked into triton stable branch, to make updates easier.

🐛 Describe the bug
I use the hugging face transformers and the DistilBert specifically. However, torch.compile fails because of it. The code associated with the bug:
from typing import List, Union
import pytorch_lightning as pl

import torch.nn as nn
import os

import torch
from torch import Tensor
from torch.distributions.distribution import Distribution
import hydra


class DistilbertEncoderBase(pl.LightningModule):
    def __init__(self, modelpath: str, finetune: bool = False) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel
        from transformers import logging
        logging.set_verbosity_error()
        # Tokenizer
        os.environ["TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM"] = "false"
        # workaround to work from cluster and local
        rel_p = modelpath.split('/')
        rel_p = rel_p[rel_p.index('deps'):]
        rel_p = '/'.join(rel_p)
        modelpath = hydra.utils.get_original_cwd() + '/' + rel_p

        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(modelpath)

        # Text model
        self.text_model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(modelpath)
        # Don't train the model
        if not finetune:
            self.text_model.training = False
            # for p in self.text_model.parameters():
            #     p.requires_grad = False

        # Then configure the model
        self.text_encoded_dim = self.text_model.config.dim
        self.finetune = finetune

    def train(self, mode: bool = True):
        self.training = mode
        for module in self.children():
            # Don't put the model in
            if module == self.text_model and not self.finetune:
                continue
            module.train(mode)
        return self

    def get_last_hidden_state(
            self,
            texts: List[str],
            return_mask: bool = False) -> Union[Tensor, tuple[Tensor, Tensor]]:
        encoded_inputs = self.tokenizer(texts,
                                        return_tensors="pt",
                                        padding=True)
        output = self.text_model(**encoded_inputs.to(self.text_model.device))
        if not return_mask:
            return output.last_hidden_state
        return output.last_hidden_state, encoded_inputs.attention_mask.to(
            dtype=bool)

When trying to run BEiT V2 with the new model.compile function I seem to get a segmentation fault. I reproduced with stock repository.
You can see my fork of unilm here. You can use the conda environment beit2/environment.yml.

cd <unilm_path>/beit2/semantic_segmentation; python tools/train.py configs/beit/upernet/upernet_beit_base_12_512_slide_160k_21ktoade20k.py --work-dir /tmp/beit2_test/
This command fails when I uncomment the model.compile in beit2/semantic_segmentation/mmcv_custom/train_api.py:86 with a segmentation fault.

nodes.title: Inconsistent results when mutating a tensor with shared storage in a nested function

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
If I define two fc layers, it should generate the same matrix no matter how many times I run. But if I delete the later fc layer, it appears that it cannot generate the same matrix as before.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# set seed
torch.manual_seed(0)
print(torch.initial_seed())

class model(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=3, out_features=2, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(in_features=3, out_features=3, bias=False)

        self.reset_parameters()


    def reset_parameters(self):
        torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(self.fc1.weight.data, gain=1)
        torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(self.fc2.weight.data, gain=1)

m = model().to('cuda')

print(m.fc1.weight.data)
print(m.fc2.weight.data)
print(torch.initial_seed())
result:
$$ python3 test_reset.py
0
tensor([[ 0.3817,  0.5129, -0.0285],
        [ 0.5564,  0.6629, -0.0281]], device='cuda:0')
tensor([[-0.4174,  1.6549, -0.3265],
        [ 0.0926, -0.0146,  0.6200],
        [ 1.3065, -0.5297, -0.1300]], device='cuda:0')
0
when I delete self.fc2:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# set seed
torch.manual_seed(0)
print(torch.initial_seed())

class model(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(in_features=3, out_features=2, bias=False)
        # self.fc2 = nn.Linear(in_features=3, out_features=3, bias=False)

        self.reset_parameters()


    def reset_parameters(self):
        torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(self.fc1.weight.data, gain=1)
        # torch.nn.init.xavier_normal_(self.fc2.weight.data, gain=1)

m = model().to('cuda')

print(m.fc1.weight.data)
# print(m.fc2.weight.data)
print(torch.initial_seed())
result:
$$ python3 test_reset.py
0
tensor([[ 0.7997, -0.4348,  0.1014],
        [-0.3836, -0.4953,  0.6718]], device='cuda:0')
0
You can see that this fc1 layer has the same size and the same seed, but those two layers do not have the same random matrix.
I do not know whether this is a deliberately added feature or a bug. If this is a bug, I think there may be something wrong with tensor.uniform_().

nodes.title: [CPU Inductor] Compiler error in floating-point operations involving tensors converted from int

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
The demo code:
from mmengine.dist import all_gather, broadcast, get_rank, init_dist

import torch


def batch_shuffle_ddp(x: torch.Tensor):
    """Batch shuffle, for making use of BatchNorm.
    Args:
        x (torch.Tensor): Data in each GPU.
    Returns:
        Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: Output of shuffle operation.
            - x_gather[idx_this]: Shuffled data.
            - idx_unshuffle: Index for restoring.
    """
    # gather from all gpus
    batch_size_this = x.shape[0]
    x_gather = torch.cat(all_gather(x), dim=0)
    batch_size_all = x_gather.shape[0]

    num_gpus = batch_size_all // batch_size_this

    # random shuffle index
    idx_shuffle = torch.randperm(batch_size_all)

    # broadcast to all gpus
    broadcast(idx_shuffle, src=0)

    # index for restoring
    idx_unshuffle = torch.argsort(idx_shuffle)

    # shuffled index for this gpu
    gpu_idx = get_rank()
    idx_this = idx_shuffle.view(num_gpus, -1)[gpu_idx]

    return x_gather[idx_this], idx_unshuffle


if __name__ == '__main__':
    init_dist(launcher='pytorch')
    func = torch.compile(batch_shuffle_ddp)
    func(torch.ones(1, 1, 1, 1))

🐛 Describe the bug
For a module with 2 following up conv_add_relu fusion patterns (rn50 also has these patterns), We find only one of the conv_add_relu pattern has been matched by the Quantization 2.0 frontend by printing matches_without_qconfig   in the prepare function. Here is the example code to reproduce this issue.
A small example module could be:
class Mod(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self,) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels=3, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False
        )
        self.maxpool = torch.nn.MaxPool2d(2)
        self.conv2 = torch.nn.Conv2d(in_channels=16, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.conv3 = torch.nn.Conv2d(in_channels=16, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=True)
        self.relu = torch.nn.ReLU()

        self.conv4 = torch.nn.Conv2d(in_channels=16, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=True)
        self.relu2 = torch.nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        x1 = self.conv(x)
        res1 = self.relu(self.conv2(x1) + self.conv3(x1))
        res2 = self.relu2(self.conv4(res1) + res1)
        return res2

nodes.title: torch dynamo optimization

nodes.bodyText:
Overview
This is a feature request for a version of _apply() that does not call recursively and instead only applies to the target module, not its submodules. In other words, it skips the first two lines in its current implementation:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/modules/module.py
    
    
        Lines 795 to 797
      in
      985fc66
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def _apply(self, fn): 
        

        
          
               for module in self.children(): 
        

        
          
                   module._apply(fn) 
        
    
  


For parameter offloading schemes, modules' parameters may no longer have uniform device. Being able to call an API similar to the existing .to() but only applying to a target module and not its submodules facilitates clean parameter offloading implementations.
Case Study: FullyShardedDataParallel
When a user passes both cpu_offload=CPUOffload(True) and device_id to PyTorch FullyShardedDataParallel (FSDP), where there are nested FSDP instances, FSDP calls module.to(device), which incorrectly moves all module's parameters to device including submodules whose parameters have already been offloaded to CPU. This greatly reduces the model size that FSDP can support because already sharded parameters in submodules are moved to GPU when they should stay on CPU. The device_id argument can help speed up FSDP initialization when CPU offloading is enabled since the flattening and sharding happens on GPU, not CPU.
We want to replace the module.to(device) call with a version that traverses module.modules() but does not proceed into any existing FSDP module and only moves the traversed modules to device. This is where the non-recursive _apply() / to() helps. Then, we will be able to support much larger models with CPU offloading enabled and device_id specified.
API
Since _apply() is the basis for several public frontends like .to(), .cuda(), .cpu(), adding a recurse: bool argument to all may be a sweeping change. Hence, another option is to have a private API like _apply_non_recursive(fn) that subsumes the current _apply() implementation minus the first two lines:
def _apply_non_recursive(fn):
    # Current `_apply()` implementation minus first two lines
    ...

def _apply(fn):
    for module in self.children(): 
        module._apply(fn)
    return _apply_non_recursive(fn)

Alternatively, we (the distributed team) could effectively fork the current _apply() implementation in distributed code to unblock our FSDP use case. Regardless, any alternative seems to require peaking into the module._parameters dict ourselves.
cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki
